extracted.intended_audience: IP practitioners, patent & trademark attorneys and in-house counsel (Brazil and Colombia)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and legal standards for prosecution and litigation of patents (and related trademark rules) in Brazil and Colombia, covering patentability, filing formalities, claim drafting, enforcement remedies, procedural options, and related regulatory regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate practice (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The losing party has the right to file an appeal before the appellate court (de novo review); further appeals can be filed before the Superior Court of Justice if the lower court decision violates federal statutes and before the Supreme Court if it violates the Constitution. Certain interlocutory decisions (e.g., granting or rejecting a request for preliminary injunctive relief) can be challenged by interlocutory appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interlocutory appeals are available for key preliminary rulings; appellate review may be available on statutory and constitutional grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement and alternative dispute resolution (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may voluntarily settle infringement cases. Parties can only settle invalidity lawsuits if the Brazilian PTO, a mandatory co-defendant, agrees with the settlement. Mediation and arbitration are widely available but rarely used in infringement and invalidity actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement hearings are often a pre-trial mandatory proceeding; ensure PTO consent for invalidity settlements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee shifting (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The losing party is normally ordered to pay a certain amount as attorney fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts established by the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure and set by the judge are typically a very small fraction of actual attorney charges; budget accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal liability upon finding of infringement (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No personal liability except in criminal cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust risk when enforcing IP (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sham litigation complaints have been filed before Brazilian Antitrust Authorities by defendants accused of patent (and other IP) infringement; antitrust complaints have been used in standard-essential technology disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent/trademark owners should frame enforcement to minimize antitrust risk; past decisions show significant exposure (e.g., large fines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant treaties and conventions (trademarks & patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists treaties and conventions that inform prosecution and protection (e.g., TRIPS, Paris Convention, Nice and Vienna Classification Agreements, PCT, Budapest Treaty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These international instruments shape eligibility, filing, deposit and recognition requirements; practitioners must account for them in cross-border strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of trademarks (registrable forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominative, figurative, combined and three-dimensional signs can be registered as trademarks; visually perceptive distinctive signs are susceptible of registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audible, olfactory and taste signs cannot be registered in Brazil since statute provides protection only for visually perceptive signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness and confusing similarity criteria (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks must be sufficiently distinct in comparison to other signs. Criteria analyze ideological, phonetic and visual elements, considering the specific class and prior coexistence in the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is comparative and context-specific to class and marketplace coexistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unregistrable marks (comprehensive prohibitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long statutory list of signs prohibited from registration (items I–XXIII), including official crests and flags, isolated letters/digits (unless sufficiently distinctive), expressions contrary to morals/good customs, public entity designations (unless requested by that entity), reproductions of official currency, signs likely to cause confusion with third-party names or marks, generic/descriptive signs, advertising-only expressions, colors (unless arranged distinctively), geographic indications, false indications of origin/quality, reproductions of registered collective/certification marks, names/prizes/symbols of official events (unless authorized), personal names/signatures/images of third parties without consent, well-known pseudonyms without consent, copyrighted works/titles without consent, technical terms used in industry, imitations of third-party marks likely to cause confusion, duplications of a proprietor's marks for same goods/services (unless sufficiently distinctive), necessary/common shapes of products or packaging, objects protected by industrial design registrations, and signs that the applicant obviously should have known belong to a third party domiciled nationally or in a country with reciprocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each prohibition includes exceptions when consent is given or when sufficient distinctiveness exists; practitioners must check the statutory list against their mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Famous and well-known marks protection (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marks considered famous in Brazil are guaranteed special protection in all fields of activity. Well-known marks in their field (per Paris Convention) enjoy special protection independently of whether they have been previously filed or registered in Brazil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protection follows Paris Convention and TRIPS rules; registration is not prerequisite for well-known mark protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Previous user rights (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who in good faith at the date of priority or application was using an identical or similar mark for at least six months in the country will have preferential right to registration. This right can only be claimed in an opposition proceeding; previous user has 60 days from publication of a new trademark application to file an opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good-faith use and timing are critical; use opposition window to assert prior-user rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical indications (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical indications cannot be registered as trademarks but are protectable under a special title granted by the Brazilian PTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the special GI regime rather than trademark registration for geographic indications.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME criteria and fee reductions (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees charged by the Brazilian PTO are up to 60% lower for natural persons, local small companies, research institutions, NGOs, and government entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify applicant category at filing to claim applicable fee reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition system (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-grant and post-grant opposition procedures available. After filing, applications are published; third parties have 60 days to file pre-grant oppositions. Post-grant oppositions may be initiated within 6 months from grant. A decision by the Brazilian PTO is final and can only be challenged in courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants will have 60 days to respond to pre-grant oppositions once published; post-grant oppositions trigger PTO notification and 60-day response windows; plan prosecution and enforcement accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews (trademarks and patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and may increase the chances of obtaining registration. In Colombia, interviews are easy to obtain and highly recommended for patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews proactively to facilitate prosecution and clarify issues with examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection provided by pending trademark applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Brazilian IP Statute guarantees a certain level of protection arising from pending applications by establishing that the applicant has the right to take care for the integrity and reputation of the mark covered by the application. Unregistered trademarks are also protected based on unfair competition provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pending application confers some protection; rely on unfair competition law when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain name registration regime (Brazil)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain names can be easily registered; the regulator is the Internet Steering Committee (CGI.br) and Registro.br handles registrations. Domain names are registered on a first-to-file basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain name strategy should mirror first-to-file rules; register early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark infringement scope and acts (litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark registration provides the owner with the exclusive right to use the trademark; reproducing a registered mark, importing, exporting, selling, offering for sale, hiding or storing products with equal or similar registered marks may be infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both civil and criminal actions available to stop infringement; choose forum according to goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical stages of a trademark infringement action (procedural options)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation and filing of complaint and request for preliminary ex parte injunctive relief; decision on injunction; service of complaint and mandatory settlement hearing; defendant response; plaintiff reply; production of evidence; closing arguments; decision on merits; appeals as applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary ex parte injunctions and mandatory settlement hearings are common; anticipate interlocutory strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing to sue (trademark)
rubrics_metrics.description: The trademark owner – and, under certain circumstances, the licensee – has standing to file a trademark infringement action. Declaratory judgment actions of non-infringement are also available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensing agreements should clarify enforcement rights; declaratory suits can be used as forum-shopping or pre-emptive strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge's level of IP expertise (litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions have specialized business courts experienced with IP; many courts/judges have little expertise in trademark law and practitioners often must educate the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to explain basics of trademark law in chambers and briefs; use expert evidence and clear exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation delay expectations (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: No official statistics; depends on jurisdiction and case complexity. Preliminary ex parte injunction decisions may take 24 hours to a couple of weeks. Trial court merits decisions typically take 1–3 years. Appellate courts typically take 1–3 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan enforcement timeline and costs with multi-year horizons in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations and limits on damage claims (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: IP Statute (1996) specifically regulates statute of limitations for IP infringement actions as 5 years. Civil Code (2002) establishes 3 years for lawsuits seeking damages. Courts are unsettled on whether 3 or 5 years applies. Statute of limitations for filing invalidity lawsuit is 5 years from date registration is granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conservative and file claims promptly; monitor court treatment of the conflict between statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary ex parte injunctive relief requirements (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain preliminary ex parte injunctive relief the plaintiff must show likelihood of prevailing on the merits and that the plaintiff may suffer irreparable harm if injunctive relief is not granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare strong evidence of both likelihood and irreparable harm; ex parte relief can be obtained quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonds for injunctions (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Posting a bond is not a requirement for obtaining preliminary ex parte injunctive relief. However, a judge has discretion to request a bond to cover harms caused by the injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to post bond if judge requests it; include this contingency in enforcement budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revocation and interlocutory relief (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: If trial court grants preliminary injunctive relief, the defendant can file an interlocutory appeal to stay effects and request revocation, or file a motion for reconsideration before the judge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for swift interlocutory defensive actions; injunctions are reversible pending appeal in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing and procedure for trademark invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Brazilian PTO or any person with legitimate interest can file an invalidity action. Brazil has a bifurcated system: invalidity actions are decided by federal district courts (PTO is mandatory co-defendant) and must be filed within 5 years from registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity litigation is separate from infringement and must meet procedural timing rules; account for PTO involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery and evidence preservation (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no US-style discovery. Federal Rules for Civil Procedure establish possibilities for obtaining/preserving evidence such as search and seizure of infringing products or accounting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available evidence preservation tools early; plan around limited discovery rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary support and burden of proof (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may produce witness testimony, expert opinions, documentary evidence, depositions, site inspections, etc. Typically, the burden of proof lies on the plaintiff. In an invalidity lawsuit, if the Brazilian PTO sides with the plaintiff, the defendant may have a de facto burden of establishing requirements for registration. Parties can submit as many expert opinions or surveys as they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically use experts and documentary evidence; anticipate burden shifts in invalidity contexts where PTO opinion favors plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculation of damages (trademarks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages can be calculated based on (i) lost profits, (ii) profits made by the defendant, or (iii) reasonable royalties, whichever is more favorable for the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare financial and accounting evidence to support the most favorable measure for the claimant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-eligible patent subject-matter (Colombia/Andean Decision 486)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-eligible subject-matter listed in Articles 15, 20 and 21 of Decision 486 includes software per se, business methods, naturally occurring matter, methods of treatments and second uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to emphasize technical contributions and product/process claims when possible; avoid claiming software 'per se'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted for inventions corresponding to products or methods fulfilling the requirements of novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability (Article 14 of Decision 486).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure specification and claims support novelty, inventive step, and industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility models and industrial designs (patents adjuncts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models require only novelty and industrial applicability (term 10 years) and are limited to improved devices (not methods or compositions). Industrial designs protect ornamental or aesthetic aspects (term 10 years); design applications are not examined and registration is essentially automatic unless opposition or evident lack of novelty is detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider utility model/design filings when appropriate for faster/cheaper protection of devices or ornamental features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush claim practice (pharma patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markush claims are an acceptable claim format in Colombia. Examiners frequently request limiting the scope of Markush formulas to a reasonable generalization of the examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to justify breadth of Markush groups and to narrow during prosecution if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological material deposit requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A deposit of biological material is required when the invention relates to biological material and the invention cannot be adequately described to be understood/reproduced by a skilled person. The deposit must occur on or before the priority date. Deposits must allow third parties to obtain samples upon publication, and should be filed before authorities recognized under the Budapest Treaty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make deposits timely (on/before priority date) with Budapest-recognized authorities and include deposit info in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linkage system and medicines data standard (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: No US-style Orange Book linkage system exists. Resolution 3166/2015 defines a Medicaments Data Standard (MDS) creating a Unique Medicines Identifier that correlates common name with brand and commercial presentation and requires disclosure of patents covering medicines, potentially facilitating linkage-like scenarios.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track the MDS/NPIS disclosures as they may make patent listings and infringement scenarios easier to detect and enforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software patents (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Software as such (lines of code) is non-eligible subject-matter, but inventions providing a technical contribution, complying with patentability requirements and claimable as a product or process can be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame software-related inventions in terms of technical contributions and tangible product/process steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and inventive step determination
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is novel when not part of the prior art (worldwide disclosures before priority date). For novelty, earlier Colombian pending patent applications that are eventually published count as prior art. Applicant has a 12-month grace period against disclosures attributable to the inventor/assignee or certain unlawful disclosures by national offices or third parties obtaining info from the inventor. Inventive step assessed if not obvious to a person skilled in the art, usually using the EPO problem-solution approach. Evidence of unexpected/surprising results and secondary indicia of non-obviousness may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect experimental/secondary indicia evidence when possible; use problem-solution framing to argue inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of claims (claim drafting recommendations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid functional characteristics and results to be achieved when drafting claims. Article 30 of Decision 486 requires clear and concise claims, entirely supported by the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims are supported directly by specification text; limit functional claiming and always provide enabling description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and process claim drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: For methods, key point is to have the inventive steps well defined and characterized. Examiners usually request execution details in the claims (environmental or processing conditions and materials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete execution parameters and materials in claims and description to satisfy examiner requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent application formalities (required items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification; one or more drawings (if necessary); title; one or more claims; abstract; power of attorney; payment of fees; copy of applicable genetic resources access contract (if claimed products/methods developed from such resources); copy of traditional knowledge access contract (if applicable); copy of biological deposit certificate (if applicable); copy of assignment; status of foreign patent applications for same subject-matter (if available). Items marked with an asterisk are requested to obtain a filing date; remaining items can be filed later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure asterisked items are filed to obtain a filing date; avoid presenting multiple unrelated inventions in one application to prevent restriction/election requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single invention requirement / restriction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application shall only contain one invention or a group of closely related inventions. Otherwise, a restriction requirement requesting an election will be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure claims to present a single inventive concept or closely related group; be prepared to elect and file divisionals if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution timeline and costs (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent prosecution in Colombia currently lasts about 23 months (CPO is the second fastest office in the world). Costs for a typical patent process range from USD 2,500 to USD 8,000 (official and professional fees), according to complexity and number of office actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget prosecution timelines and costs accordingly; consider PPH and diligent prosecution to accelerate when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME discounts for patent filings (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular Única of the CPO provides discounts: 25% discount for natural persons without financial means, small and medium entities, certain Colombian universities and R&D foundations/nonprofits; foreign universities in co-ownership with such entities may apply for 15% discount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess eligibility at filing to claim reduced official fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: No protection by pending patent applications (Colombia)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no protection provided by pending applications. Patent rights in Colombia (and the Andean Community) can only be enforced once the patent has been granted. However, once granted, the patent owner can request damages generated by acts of infringement occurring from the date of publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement begins post-grant, but damages may be claimed for infringing acts from publication date once patent issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term and term extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent term is 20 years from the filing (or from the international filing date for PCT national phase). Decree 1873 of 2014 provides term extensions if prosecution lasted more than 5 years from filing or 3 years from examination request; pharmaceuticals are expressly excluded from extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track prosecution durations and examination request dates to evaluate extension eligibility; do not expect pharma extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition system (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colombia provides a pre-grant opposition system. Interested third parties may file an opposition within 60 days following publication of the application (extendable for the same term upon request). The CPO must consider arguments and evidence provided in an opposition during examination. There is no separate or independent opposition procedure and oppositions generally do not introduce delays exceeding 2–3 months. Third parties may file observations anytime before final decision, but Office is optional in considering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor publications closely and prepare oppositions or observations within windows; anticipate limited delay impact on prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner interviews are allowed and easy to obtain (simply request a meeting at the CPO office). Interviews are highly recommended as they are useful in many cases to facilitate prosecution and grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to clarify claim scope and expedite resolution of objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expedited examination and PPH availability
rubrics_metrics.description: No laws providing accelerated examination although diligent prosecution can reduce terms. One can request examination as soon as the application is published. Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH) programs are available with many offices (EPO, Japan, Korea, Spain, US and Pacific Alliance countries), though implementation regulations may vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PPH where possible and request early examination to shorten prosecution timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim amendments practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications are not available under Andean Decision 486. Voluntary claim amendments are possible anytime during prosecution and in any case before a final decision. If the patent is rejected, claims can be amended by filing a Reconsideration Action. Amendments cannot extend the original scope of the invention and must find support in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all amendments are fully supported by the original disclosure; plan claim amendment strategy during prosecution to avoid over-broadening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional practice (CPO Resolution 3719)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisionals may be filed at any time during prosecution, even after a non-final rejection. Parent claim sets must explicitly carve out the divisional's claimed subject matter. Claims in parent and divisional can be further amended after filing. Specification of the divisional should be adapted to reflect subject-matter divided out. Divisionals from divisionals are not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing divisionals, ensure parent claims carve out divisional subject matter and adapt the divisional specification; plan family strategy given no chain divisionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement scope and literal infringement rule (patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent protects a product, the owner can prevent third parties from importing, using, manufacturing, offering for sale or selling the product. For method patents, the owner can prevent third parties from using the method or performing acts involving products obtained directly through the protected method. A patent will be infringed if any of its claims read on an allegedly infringing product or process. Only literal infringement is contemplated under Andean Decision 486; doctrine of equivalents has not been recognized, though judges may expand interpretations equitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims carefully to cover intended infringing scenarios; do not rely on doctrine of equivalents as a primary enforcement theory.
